content: Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) is a chronic and relapsing condition affecting the gastrointestinal (GI) tract. It is believed to result from a complex interaction between the immune system, the lining of the GI tract, environmental factors, and the gut microbiome. This interplay leads to an abnormal inflammatory response in individuals with a genetic predisposition. A disruption in the normal composition of the gut microbiota, referred to as dysbiosis, is thought to play a significant role in the development of ulcerative colitis (UC) and Crohn’s disease (CD), the two main subtypes of IBD. Fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT), which involves transferring stool containing healthy gut microbiota from a donor to a recipient, has gained attention as a potential method to correct this dysbiosis. The objective of this study was to assess the benefits and safety of FMT in treating IBD in both adults and children. Comparisons were made between FMT and other interventions, including autologous FMT (using the patient’s own stool), placebo, standard medications, or no treatment. The researchers conducted a comprehensive search of databases, clinical trial registries, and reference lists of published studies up to December 22, 2022. They included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that investigated the use of FMT in individuals with UC or CD. The primary outcomes of interest were the induction of clinical remission, maintenance of clinical remission, and the occurrence of serious adverse events. Secondary outcomes included any adverse events, endoscopic remission, quality of life, clinical response, endoscopic response, withdrawal rates, inflammatory markers, and microbiome-related outcomes. The certainty of the evidence was evaluated using the GRADE approach. A total of 12 studies involving 550 participants were included in the analysis. These studies were conducted in various countries, including Australia, Canada, China, the Czech Republic, France, India, the Netherlands, the USA, Israel, and Italy. FMT was administered in different forms, such as capsules or suspensions, and delivered via oral ingestion, nasoduodenal tube, enema, or colonoscopy. One study used both oral capsules and colonoscopy for FMT delivery. Six studies were deemed to have a low risk of bias, while the remaining studies had either unclear or high risk of bias. Ten studies, involving 468 participants (nine studies on adults and one on children), evaluated the induction of clinical remission in UC over follow-up periods ranging from 6 to 12 weeks. The findings suggested that FMT may increase the likelihood of achieving clinical remission in UC compared to control interventions (risk ratio [RR] 1.79, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.13 to 2.84; low-certainty evidence). Five studies also indicated that FMT might improve rates of endoscopic remission in UC over follow-up periods of 8 to 12 weeks, but the confidence intervals were wide and included the possibility of no effect (RR 1.45, 95% CI 0.64 to 3.29; low-certainty evidence). Nine studies with 417 participants suggested that FMT may result in little to no difference in the rates of any adverse events (RR 0.99, 95% CI 0.85 to 1.16; low-certainty evidence). However, the evidence was very uncertain regarding the risk of serious adverse events (RR 1.77, 95% CI 0.88 to 3.55; very low-certainty evidence) and improvements in quality of life (mean difference [MD] 15.34, 95% CI −3.84 to 34.52; very low-certainty evidence) when FMT was used to induce remission in UC. Two studies, one of which also provided data on induction of remission in active UC, examined the use of FMT for maintaining remission in individuals with controlled UC over follow-up periods of 48 to 56 weeks. The evidence was very uncertain regarding the effectiveness of FMT in maintaining clinical remission (RR 2.97, 95% CI 0.26 to 34.42; very low-certainty evidence) or endoscopic remission (RR 3.28, 95% CI 0.73 to 14.74; very low-certainty evidence). Similarly, the evidence was very uncertain about the risk of serious or any adverse events and improvements in quality of life when FMT was used for maintenance of remission in UC. None of the included studies evaluated the use of FMT for inducing remission in individuals with CD. One study, involving 21 participants, provided data on the use of FMT for maintaining remission in CD over a 24-week period. The evidence was very uncertain regarding the effectiveness of FMT in maintaining clinical remission in CD (RR 1.21, 95% CI 0.36 to 4.14; very low-certainty evidence). Additionally, the evidence was very uncertain about the risk of serious or any adverse events when FMT was used for this purpose. None of the studies reported data on the use of FMT for maintaining endoscopic remission or improving quality of life in individuals with CD. In conclusion, FMT may increase the proportion of individuals with active UC who achieve clinical and endoscopic remission. However, the evidence is very uncertain regarding the impact of FMT on the risk of serious adverse events or improvements in quality of life in individuals with active UC. Similarly, the evidence is very uncertain about the use of FMT for maintaining remission in UC, as well as for inducing or maintaining remission in CD. No definitive conclusions can be drawn at this time. Further research is needed to better understand the potential benefits and safety of FMT in both adults and children with active UC and CD, as well as its role in promoting long-term maintenance of remission in these conditions.
